title: BSD 11 — Test
src: Jaundice, Viral Hepatitis & Sickle Cell Disease

mcqs.q: Jaundice is a yellow discoloration caused by the deposition of:
mcqs.explain: Jaundice is yellowing of skin, mucous membranes and sclera from deposition of the bile pigment bilirubin.

mcqs.q: Jaundice becomes clinically detectable once the serum bilirubin rises above:
mcqs.explain: Discoloration is clinically detectable once serum bilirubin exceeds about 2.5 mg/dL (40 µmol/L).

mcqs.q: PRE-hepatic jaundice is caused by:
opts: Excess haemolysis (e.g. sickle cell, thalassaemia, transfusion reaction)
mcqs.explain: Pre-hepatic jaundice results from excess haemolysis (sickle cell, thalassaemia, autoimmune, transfusion reactions).

mcqs.q: Obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice is characterised by:
opts: Pale/clay stools, dark (tea-coloured) urine and severe itching
Normal urine and stool with no itching
mcqs.explain: Obstruction (gallstones, stricture, tumour) gives pale/clay stools, tea-coloured urine and severe itching.

mcqs.q: In PRE-hepatic (haemolytic) jaundice, the urine and stool are:
mcqs.explain: In pre-hepatic jaundice, urine and stool colour are normal and there is no itching (the bilirubin is unconjugated).

mcqs.q: Hepatocellular jaundice is typically caused by:
opts: A gallstone in the common bile duct
mcqs.explain: Hepatocellular jaundice arises from liver-cell disease — hepatitis, cirrhosis, drugs, cancer or congenital disorders — with tea-coloured urine and mild itching.

mcqs.q: Reddening of the palms in chronic liver disease is termed:
mcqs.explain: Palmar erythema is a stigma of chronic liver disease, along with spider naevi, clubbing and Dupuytren's contracture.

mcqs.q: The vascular skin lesions with a central arteriole and radiating vessels in liver disease are:
mcqs.explain: Spider naevi (spider telangiectasias) are a classic stigma of chronic liver disease, reflecting high oestrogen.

mcqs.q: White discoloration of the nails (leukonychia) in liver disease reflects:
mcqs.explain: Leukonychia results from hypoalbuminaemia (the liver makes less albumin).

mcqs.q: Asterixis (a flapping tremor) in a jaundiced patient indicates:
mcqs.explain: Asterixis and a poor mental status point to hepatic encephalopathy in advanced liver disease.

mcqs.q: Gynaecomastia, loss of body hair and testicular atrophy in chronic liver disease are due to:
opts: A high oestrogen level (impaired hepatic metabolism)
mcqs.explain: The failing liver does not metabolise oestrogen, so a high oestrogen level causes gynaecomastia, body-hair loss and testicular atrophy.

mcqs.q: Finger clubbing in a patient with jaundice is a sign of:
mcqs.explain: Clubbing is one of the recognised stigmata of chronic liver disease, along with leukonychia and palmar erythema.

mcqs.q: To investigate suspected haemolysis as a cause of jaundice, you would check:
mcqs.explain: Haemolysis is assessed with reticulocyte count, LDH and haptoglobin (plus the unconjugated bilirubin fraction).

mcqs.q: Which imaging is used to evaluate the biliary tree in obstructive jaundice?
mcqs.explain: Ultrasound is first-line; MRCP and ERCP further evaluate (and ERCP can treat) biliary obstruction.

mcqs.q: Why is the conjugated/unconjugated bilirubin split useful in jaundice?
opts: It helps distinguish pre-hepatic (unconjugated) from obstructive/hepatic (conjugated) causes
mcqs.explain: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia points to haemolysis (pre-hepatic), while conjugated points to hepatocellular/obstructive disease.

mcqs.q: An oral mucosal condition associated with hepatitis B and C infection is:
mcqs.explain: Lichen planus, Sjögren's syndrome and sialadenitis are associated with HBV/HCV infection.

mcqs.q: Hepatitis B is mainly transmitted in the dental office via:
opts: Blood (and saliva); unvaccinated staff have a 10× risk
mcqs.explain: HBV is blood-borne (and present in saliva); unvaccinated dental staff have a 10× greater occupational risk, so vaccination and barriers are essential.

mcqs.q: After a needlestick from an unvaccinated worker, specific prophylaxis includes:
opts: Starting the HBV vaccine series and giving HBIG within 24 hours
mcqs.explain: Begin the HBV vaccine series (0, 1, 6 months) and give HBIG as soon as possible (within 24 h) at a separate site.

mcqs.q: When treating a known hepatitis carrier, surfaces should be disinfected with:
mcqs.explain: Working/environmental surfaces are wiped with 2% activated glutaraldehyde (Cidex); full barrier technique and aseptic measures are used throughout.

mcqs.q: Sickle cell disease causes which TYPE of jaundice?
mcqs.explain: Chronic haemolysis in sickle cell disease produces pre-hepatic (unconjugated) jaundice.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised dental complication of sickle cell disease?
opts: Pulp necrosis (and caries, hypodontia, malocclusion, abnormal trabeculae)
mcqs.explain: Sickle cell dental complications include caries, erosions, pulp necrosis, hypodontia, malocclusion, abnormal trabecular spacing and infection.

mcqs.q: The preferred analgesia for a sickle cell patient is:
mcqs.explain: Paracetamol + codeine (and morphine derivatives) are preferred; aspirin is avoided as it risks acidosis and can precipitate a crisis.

mcqs.q: Why are infections treated especially vigorously in sickle cell patients?
opts: Infection can precipitate a sickle crisis
mcqs.explain: Any dental or non-dental infection must be treated vigorously, since infection can trigger a vaso-occlusive crisis; prophylactic antibiotics are used for surgery.

mcqs.q: When extraction is needed in a sickle cell patient, special care is taken because:
opts: The bone is fragile/osteoporotic, with a risk of osteonecrosis
mcqs.explain: Extraction must protect the fragile, osteoporotic bone from fracture and reduce the risk of future osteonecrosis from traumatic extraction.

saqs.q: Define jaundice and give its detection threshold.
saqs.a: Yellowing of the skin, mucous membranes and sclera from deposition of bilirubin; clinically detectable once serum bilirubin exceeds 2.5 mg/dL (40 µmol/L).

saqs.q: Classify jaundice with the urine, stool and itching pattern.
saqs.a: Pre-hepatic (haemolytic): normal urine/stool, no itch. Hepatocellular: tea urine, mild itch. Obstructive: tea urine, pale stools, severe itch.

saqs.q: List the stigmata of chronic liver disease.
saqs.a: Palmar erythema, spider naevi, clubbing, leukonychia (hypoalbuminaemia), bruising, asterixis (encephalopathy), gynaecomastia/testicular atrophy (high oestrogen), ascites.

saqs.q: Which investigations distinguish the cause of jaundice?
saqs.a: Conjugated/unconjugated bilirubin, AST/ALT/ALP, INR, albumin; reticulocytes/LDH/haptoglobin for haemolysis; viral serology (HBsAg, anti-HCV); imaging (US, MRCP/ERCP), biopsy.

saqs.q: What are the oral and occupational concerns of viral hepatitis?
saqs.a: Oral: lichen planus, sialadenitis, gingival bleeding (cirrhotic thrombocytopenia). Occupational: HBV/HCV are blood-borne; unvaccinated staff have a 10× HBV risk — vaccinate and use barriers.

saqs.q: Outline post-exposure prophylaxis after a needlestick.
saqs.a: Wash with soap & water (no antiseptics in wound), report/document, test the source (HBsAg/HCV/HIV), and give the HBV vaccine series + HBIG within 24 h for the unvaccinated.

saqs.q: Summarise the dental management of a sickle cell patient.
saqs.a: Analgesia: paracetamol + codeine (avoid aspirin → acidosis/crisis). Treat all infections vigorously; prophylactic antibiotics for surgery; extract carefully to protect fragile osteoporotic bone (osteonecrosis risk).
